## The problem

Research teams deciding where a new systematic review is needed can't manually read thousands of abstracts to see which areas of primary research the existing reviews haven't covered.

## Approach

PubMed Entrez query split by publication type (review vs non-review) -> TF-IDF (1-2 grams) -> TruncatedSVD(100) -> k-means (also DBSCAN, agglomerative, LDA; Doc2Vec/FastText options) -> cluster-level TF-IDF cosine similarity between research and review clusters -> clusters with max similarity < 0.3 flagged as candidate gaps. Batch vignettes for 5 precision-nutrition searches.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Why it matters for a decision

Supports a portfolio or prioritization decision (which topics merit a new evidence synthesis), analogous to horizon scanning of a research portfolio. Currently only valid as exploratory triage for human review.
:::

Every result above is traced to a script, log, or artifact in the repository. See [How I Check My Work](/approach.qmd).

## Limitations

- Clusters are weak and unstable: cosine silhouette 0.02-0.09 for k=2..12; median ARI across k-means seeds 0.20-0.33 on corpora under 500 papers.
- The gap score is confounded by cluster size (Spearman rho 0.52-0.93 between research-cluster size and max similarity) and by corpus size (large corpora give 0 gaps at 0.3, small ones give 3-5).
- Fails a null test: splitting research papers against themselves still flags 2 of 8 'gaps' on two searches.
- The 0.3 threshold isn't justified or calibrated, and there's no ground-truth validation.
- Similarity is vocabulary overlap of concatenated abstracts, not semantic coverage; some flagged clusters are reporting boilerplate ('group, significantly, 05').
- Results depend on the PubMed query date and on publication-type tagging; review counts differ between the query filter and the parsed flag (203 vs 217).

## Tools

Python, Streamlit, Biopython (Entrez), scikit-learn, gensim, umap-learn, Plotly
